title: A Team That Stares at the Problem Statement
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The post argues that a team wrestling with a major decision should literally keep the problem statement in view, written on a whiteboard or screen. Seeing the words makes the facets and sub-issues of the problem stand out, and it anchors the conversation to the real issue instead of tangents. Because people debate whether the wording accurately captures the root issues, the statement itself becomes a tool for surfacing root causes. The author presents this as a deceptively simple facilitation tactic whose payoff is a more open, collaborative discussion. The practical instruction is to make the visual large enough that no one can ignore it. The closing claim is that problem visuals produce clear thinking, which complex problem-solving leaders need.
points: Displaying the problem statement turns it into a shared reference point that keeps debate on the actual issue rather than tangents.
Debating the exact words of the statement is how a team tests whether it reflects the root issues.
A leader who keeps the statement front and center creates a more open and collaborative discussion.
The tactic only works if the visual is large and clear enough that it cannot be ignored.
quotes: An interesting thing happens when team members grappling with a major decision or opportunity can stare at the problem statement. The many parts or facets of the problem will stand out like flashing lights.

Different parts of the statement become magnified during the discussion. The words used to describe the problem create a focus and gather attention. Team members are then more likely to debate the meaning of those words and describe why they accurately or inaccurately reflect the root issues.

A visual representation provides a reference point for the discussion, ensuring the conversation revolves around the problem and not a tangential issue. When team members are forced to view the problem on a white board or screen, they are more likely to contribute their thinking about the complexities involved.

Simply by keeping the problem statement front and center, leaders create a more open and collaborative environment for the discussion. It's hard to fully comprehend how such a simple tactic can have such a marked impact on the group discussion, but it does.

This structured approach helps in analyzing the problem from different angles and vantage points. As team members stare at the statement, the root causes underlying the problem come into sharp relief.
But its bigger impact is with how it changes the discussion. Problem visuals create clear thinking. Leaders need all the help they can get when solving complex problems.
